Background In many cases, dental treatments need to be performed under general anesthesia. Uncooperative patients of all ages with uncontrollably high levels of dental fear or anxiety, intellectual and developmental disabilities, psychiatric problems, or mental retardation struggle to tolerate in-office dental treatment. Patients with special healthcare needs, systemic diseases, or allergies to local anesthetics are frequently treated under general anesthesia in dentistry [ 1 ]. Dental treatment under general anesthesia may be a good option for people with congenital heart problems due to lowering their risk of infective endocarditis in a single session under a single antibiotic prophylaxis [ 2 ]. Moreover, dental treatment under general anesthesia may be an inevitable option for conditions such as temporomandibular joint ankylosis, caused by trauma, surgery, infection, or arthritis [ 3 ]. General anesthesia, enabling comprehensive, pain-free, and high-quality dental care, is particularly beneficial for non-cooperative children with behavioral issues or disabilities and children with early childhood caries (ECC) [ 4 ]. Early childhood caries, typified by decay, missing, or filled teeth in the primary dentition, is a common and severe public health concern impacting millions of young children worldwide [ 5 ]. The negative impacts of poor oral health and untreated dental caries on children’s psychological and social development and overall health have been well established. Early childhood caries also negatively affects the quality of life of both children and their parents, causing problems related to pain, sleep, and nutrition. Comprehensive restorative and preventive therapies are required, as caries can spread swiftly to other teeth. Immediate intervention and rapid treatment of early childhood caries are important not only for managing its negative impacts on children but also to lessen its burden on healthcare institutions and society [ 5 ]. In the abovementioned circumstances where multisession dental treatments at a dental office are not applicable, the management of early childhood caries under general anesthesia offers full-mouth dental rehabilitation in one session in a controlled environment, reducing dental fear and anxiety in young children [ 4 , 6 ]. Evaluating dental problems and treatments should consider clinical changes and dental interventions’ impact on patients’ quality of life. The concept of measuring the change in the oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) of individuals has attracted considerable interest in recent years [ 7 , 8 ]. OHRQoL is used to assess patients’ oral health status and treatment effectiveness, determining the psychosocial effects of dental issues. It is a multidimensional concept that evaluates the physical, psychological, and social impacts of oral health conditions on individuals’ overall well-being [ 7 , 8 ]. Numerous tools have been developed for measuring OHRQoL for children [ 7 ]. The first OHRQoL tool, the Child Oral Health Quality of Life (COHRQoL) questionnaire [ 9 – 11 ], consisting of two parent-assessed components that are the Parental-Caregiver Perceptions Questionnaire (P-CPQ) and the Family Impact Scale (FIS), is answered by the parent or caregiver of 6–14-year-old children as the target group by referring to the frequency of events in the past three months. A short version of this questionnaire was later developed by Thomson et al. [ 12 ] because it was thought that its length would increase participant burden and limit routine use [ 13 ]. To assess preschool children’s (younger than six years of age) OHRQoL, Pahel et al. [ 14 ] developed the Early Childhood Oral Health Impact Scale (ECOHIS) in 2007. The ECOHIS questionnaire consists of two subscales: the Child Impact Scale (CIS) and the FIS. The ECOHIS questionnaire is answered by the parent/caregiver of 3–5-year-old children, the target group. Previously, a meta-analysis [ 15 ] assessed the studies published between 2009 and 2017, which report the change in the OHRQoL of children who received dental treatment under general anesthesia. This study suggested that there is evidence to support that children’s OHRQoL improves in the short-term following dental treatment under general anesthesia. However, many publications that deserve more systematic research have been published since this meta-analysis, and an updated assessment of the recent body of literature documenting changes in children’s OHRQoL after dental treatment under general anesthesia is needed. Therefore, the aim of this study is to conduct a meta-analysis to synthesize existing research on how dental treatments under general anesthesia affect the oral health-related quality of life in children. Methods Literature review and data sources In this paper, a meta-analysis was executed to examine the pooled available data in accordance with the “Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA)” guidelines [ 16 ]. A comprehensive search of electronic databases such as PubMed, EMBASE, Ovid MEDLINE, Web of Science (WoS), and Scopus was undertaken to identify studies that evaluate changes in OHRQoL following dental treatments under general anesthesia in children. Supp. Table S1 features the PRISMA checklist, detailing the essential criteria and guidelines utilized during the meta-analysis. This checklist provided a thorough framework, ensuring that this study-maintained clarity and conformed to the PRISMA guidelines. The data collection for this study was planned and executed to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the findings. Initially, a comprehensive database search was conducted by two independent researchers to yield relevant publications. Each researcher used predetermined, specific inclusion and exclusion criteria to filter the studies, ensuring that only those directly relevant to the research question were included. This dual-reviewer approach helped minimize bias and enhance the validity of the study selection process. After this initial phase, discrepancies between the two sets of findings were discussed and resolved through consensus, further solidifying the integrity of the data collection method. The search was started on February 20, 2024, and conducted through April 2, 2024, as well as a repeat search was conducted on April 24 to ensure the most up-to-date information available was included. In conducting the database searches, a structured approach was utilized to ensure comprehensive coverage of relevant literature. The Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, Boolean operators (AND / OR), and text words were employed in searches to effectively achieve suitable papers. In addition, the reference lists of the studies were also scanned. The primary keyword phrases, “oral health-related quality of life” OR “OHRQoL,” were combined using the Boolean operator AND with a series of terms related to the intervention focus: “dental treatment under general anesthesia,” “dental treatment under general anaesthesia,” “dental general anesthesia,” “dental general anaesthesia,” “general anesthesia,” and “general anaesthesia.” For the current meta-analysis, the literature search was restricted to publications in English. Hence, studies published in languages other than English were systematically excluded from the search. To ensure a clear and organized presentation of the search strategies employed for each relevant database, a structured form was included in the supplementary materials. This form, available as Table S2, details the specific search terms, combinations of keywords, and filters used across different databases. Study selection The Early Childhood Oral Health Impact Scale [ 14 ] questionnaire consists of 13 questions under two subscales: the Child Impact Scale (CIS) and the FIS. The CIS inquires about the parameters related to children in four domains: child symptoms (item–1), child function (items–2–5), child psychology (items–6–7), and child self-image/social interactions (items–8–9) via nine questions. The family impact scale inquires about the parameters related to children’s families in two domains: parental stress and family functioning, via four questions. The potential response to each question is scored on a 5-point Likert scale as follows: 0 for “never,” 1 for “hardly ever,” 2 for “occasionally,” 3 for “often,” and 4 for “very often.” As the respondent is the proxy of the children, whose OHRQoL was being assessed, an “I do not know” response is also offered in the questionnaire to avoid a proxy overestimation of the treatment effects. The COHRQoL [ 9 – 11 ] questionnaire originally consisted of 49 questions with parent-assessed components: the P-CPQ with 33 items, the FIS with 14 items, and two global items. Later, Thomson et al. [ 12 ] developed the short-form version of COHRQoL, consisting of 16-item PCPQ and 8-item FIS questionnaires. The short-form version of P-CPQ inquires about the impact of oral health on the patient via 16 questions under four subscales, each containing four items: oral symptoms, functional limitations, emotional well-being, and social well-being. The short-form version of FIS inquires about the impact of the patient’s oral health on the family via eight questions under three subscales: parental activities (four items), parental emotions (two items), and family conflicts (two items). The potential responses to each question in the PCPQ/FIS questionnaire are scored on a 3-point Likert scale as follows: 0 for “never,” 1 for “sometimes,” 2 for “often,” and 3 for “every day/almost every day.” The inclusion criteria for the study were established as follows: use of validated OHRQoL instruments, specifically ECOHIS, COHRQoL (P-CPQ and FIS), assessments conducted both before and after the procedure; participants aged between 0 and 16 years; no limitations regarding the duration of follow-up; and studies involving dental treatments under general anesthesia, and studies published in English. Additionally, only studies published in peer-reviewed journals were included in the study. Initially, all identified records from the database searches were screened based on their titles and abstracts to determine their preliminary relevance to the research questions. Those who met the initial criteria were then subjected to a more detailed full-text review to assess their compliance with the inclusion criteria, which included factors such as study design, participant age group, and specific outcomes related to oral health-related quality of life following dental treatment under general anesthesia. Studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria and reviews that did not present original reports, reports such as letters to the editor, and case reports were excluded from the investigation. This two-step selection process was independently conducted by two investigators (N.A.Y. and C.E.) to minimize bias and errors. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third investigator (M.E.A.) when necessary, ensuring a thorough and unbiased selection of studies for the final analysis. For organized data management and to preserve consistency, all collected data were logged into a pre-organized, structured Microsoft Excel ® spreadsheet. Data extraction and quality assessment Data extraction for the study was conducted using a structured approach to ensure accuracy and minimize bias. Each selected study was systematically analyzed, and relevant data were carefully extracted based on predefined criteria. Key information such as study design, participant demographics, details of dental treatment under general anesthesia, outcomes measured, and follow-up periods were recorded. The extracted data were then compiled into a standardized format to facilitate comparative analysis and synthesis across different studies. The Cochrane Collaboration’s tool for assessing the risk of bias was employed for the quality assessment of the included studies [ 17 ]. Many critical factors were evaluated for quality assessment. These factors comprised allocation concealment, the generation of random sequences, blinding of participants and researchers as well as outcome assessments, the completeness of the data, the potential for reporting bias, including selective reporting, and other biases. GRADING level of evidence was evaluated by the Oxford Center for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) [ 18 ]. PICOs : Population: Children receiving dental treatment under general anesthesia. Intervention: The effect of dental treatment under general anesthesia on oral health-related quality of life. Comparison: The change in oral health-related quality of life after dental treatment under general anesthesia. Outcomes: (i) ECOHIS scores; (ii) COHRQoL (P-CPQ) scores; and (iii) COHRQoL (FIS) scores. Study: A single-subject-design intervention study. Statistical analysis In this meta-analysis, the mean differences between scale measurements before and after dental treatments under general anesthesia were reported as the standard mean difference (SMD). In conducting primary (ECOHIS and COHRQoL) and secondary meta-analyses (FIS) estimates of pooled effect size between related mean differences were calculated using Hedges’s g effect size estimation and provided with a corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI). Effect sizes for Hedges’ g were classified as follows: small effect (0.2), medium effect (0.5), large effect (0.8) [ 19 ]. All meta-analysis statistical computation was executed using the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method for the random effects model [ 20 , 21 ]. A standard error correction was performed for all estimated effect sizes. To evaluate the heterogeneity of the included research, the χ2-based Cochran’s Q test and I 2 statistics were utilized; significant heterogeneity was indicated by a p-value less than 0.05 on the Cochran’s Q test and an I 2 value exceeding 50%, suggesting that the observed variations among study results were more likely due to genuine heterogeneity rather than random chance. Schematic illustrations of funnel plots for inverse standard error were provided to evaluate the potential for publication bias. The robustness of the test results was also scrutinized through sensitivity analyses. For this purpose, each study was omitted from the pooled analysis individually, and the change in test results was investigated. The sensitivity analysis results were also summarized visually. A two-sided p-value of less than 0.05 was used as the threshold for resolving statistical significance in all tests conducted. All statistical calculations during the process of conducting the meta-analysis were performed employing the STATA (v18, College Station, TX, USA) package program. Results Initial screening of the database search revealed a total of 499 papers. When detailed databases were scrutinized, it was determined that 76 of these articles were indexed in PubMed, 128 in Web of Science, 165 in Embase, 73 in Scopus, and 57 in Ovid Medline. After removing duplicate papers indexed in various databases, a total of 271 articles were checked for further examination. After an initial title and abstract review, 167 articles were excluded from meta-analysis without a full-text review. Of the remaining 104 reports, after full-text review, a total of 36 papers [ 12 , 22 – 56 ] met the inclusion criteria and were included in the investigation. The PRISMA flowchart demonstrating the search process in the relevant databases is summarized in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 PRISMA flowchart showing summary of search strategy In the primary reports included in the study, ECOHIS questionnaires were utilized in 25 studies, and COHRQoL questionnaires were used in 13 research studies. In two studies [ 35 , 56 ] reviewed, researchers administered the ECOHIS and COHRQoL questionnaires to assemble data. In one study [ 52 ], age groups were separated, and results were reported in two groups. The outcomes of this study were analyzed as two separate reports. According to the Cochrane risk of bias tool [ 57 ], since there was no control group in the planning of the studies, it was accepted that there was a risk of low performance and detection bias for all of the studies. It was observed that almost all of the studies that evaluated pre- and post-tests had a high risk of selection bias due to non-random sequence generation and allocation concealment. Studies evaluated within the framework of OCEBM [ 18 ] standards were classified at the 2B level of evidence in terms of the “hierarchy of evidence” due to the loss of follow-up for participants before and after the procedure and the lack of randomization. Detailed risk of bias evaluation results were visually provided in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Risk of bias assessment of the included research Baseline characteristics of studies In ECOHIS studies, sample sizes before and after treatment varied from a minimum of 15 to a maximum 252. The mean ages of the patients were between 2.75 (± 0.6) and 8.3 (± 3.2). The median follow-up time ranged from one week to 52.2 weeks (one year). Except one [ 26 ] study that is retrospective, all studies were prospective. All the studies, with the exception of four [ 25 , 29 , 45 , 46 ], were nonrandomized. Except for five [ 23 , 27 , 29 , 46 , 48 ], studies did not include a control group. The sample collection and communication methodology varied and included face-to-face, telephone, structured, self-administered, postal, in-person, and/or a combination of two or more methods. In 20 studies [ 1 – 3 , 7 , 11 , 12 , 16 – 23 , 25 , 29 – 31 , 35 , 36 ], dental treatment under general anesthesia was conducted only on healthy children with no systemic diseases, mental problems, or disabilities. Two studies [ 30 , 33 ] included children with special health care needs only. Three studies [ 27 , 29 , 35 ] included children who are healthy or with mild to severe systemic diseases. Twelve studies [ 2 , 5 , 11 , 19 – 21 , 24 , 25 , 27 , 31 , 33 , 34 ] did not report the type of dental treatments performed under general anesthesia. Six studies [ 15 , 18 , 28 , 29 , 32 , 35 ] provided limited data about the dental treatments. Twelve studies [ 1 , 3 , 7 – 10 , 12 , 13 , 17 , 22 , 26 , 36 ] provided clear data regarding the type of dental treatments performed. Outcomes of meta-analysis for ECOHIS scores A total of 25 studies were included in the pooled analysis for pre- and post-treatment comparisons of ECOHIS questionnaire scores. As seen in Fig. 3 , it was concluded that dental treatments under general anesthesia in children improved OHRQoL in the short term with a significantly large effect size (SMD = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.07–2.24, p < 0.001). A high level of heterogeneity was noticed among the studies included in the meta-analysis (τ 2 = 2.18, I 2 = 98.9, p < 0.001) (Fig. 3 ). In the sensitivity analysis conducted by separately excluding the reports in the pooled analysis, it was observed that one study [ 35 ] reported a relative outlier value. In the meta-analysis conducted by omitting this study, the effect size (SMD) was found to be 1.46 (95% CI: 1.18–1.74, p < 0.001), again with a large effect size. Sensitivity analysis results are presented in Supp. Figure S1 , and a funnel plot for the inverse standard error is also presented in Supp. Figure S2 . Fig. 3 The forest plot of pooled analysis results for ECOHIS scores. CI = confidence interval Outcomes of meta-analysis for COHRQoL scores In the meta-analysis conducted to compare COHRQoL questionnaire scores before and after treatment, 14 reports from a total of 13 articles were yielded for the pooled effect size. Accordingly, the pooled SMD of the COHRQoL score in children receiving dental treatment under general anesthesia was found to be 1.32 (95% CI: 0.81–1.84, p < 0.001), with a high level of heterogeneity (τ 2 = 0.78, I 2 = 97.3, p < 0.001). The forest plot of the results is demonstrated in Fig. 4 . Sensitivity analyses were also conducted to evaluate the robustness of the test results. When a study [ 35 ] reporting an outlier value was excluded from the analysis, the effect size was found to be 1.13 (95% CI: 0.88–1.37, p < 0.001) (Supp. Figure S3 ), again with a large effect size. A funnel plot for the inverse standard error for the relevant effect size is also illustrated in Supp. Figure S4 . Fig. 4 The forest plot of pooled analysis results for COHRQoL scores. As noticed in Fig. 5 , there was a high level of heterogeneity across studies (τ 2 = 0.41, I 2 = 95.6, p < 0.001). CI = confidence interval Discussion The findings of two validated and the most commonly used OHRQoL tools (ECOHIS and COHRQoL) for children were included in this meta-analysis. The pooled data indicated that dental treatments under general anesthesia significantly improved the oral health-related quality of life of children. Although all studies pointed out a significant improvement in overall OHRQoL, the change percentages for OHRQoL varied based on the individual study design of the included studies. The high level of heterogeneity can be attributed to the high diversity in the study designs and a number of factors that cannot be standardized or controlled in the study setting. These factors include patients’ age, ethnicity, initial oral health and medical status, type and complexity of dental treatments, facilities of the health centre, operator impact on the quality of dental treatments (restorations and/or interventions performed), and duration of follow-up, etc. Using a multidisciplinary approach, it is possible to establish a comprehensive full-mouth dental rehabilitation in one session under general anesthesia. An important aspect to notice is that the type and complexity of dental procedures can have an impact on patients’ post-operative comfort and OHRQoL. Therefore, it is crucial to specify the therapies or interventions administered to the patient in a study to draw conclusions about the impact of dental treatment under general anesthesia on quality of life. Several studies [ 12 , 23 , 26 , 32 , 40 – 42 , 45 , 46 , 48 , 53 , 55 ] lack information on the dental treatments administered to the patients. Some others provided limited data without describing the dental treatments in detail, namely the patients received restorative treatment, extraction-only approach, or their combination [ 36 , 39 , 49 , 50 , 52 , 54 ] was applied. Several researchers [ 22 , 24 , 28 – 31 , 33 , 34 , 38 , 43 , 47 , 56 ] provided specific descriptions of the dental treatment therapy modalities, such as resin-modified glass ionomer, compomer and composite restorations, pulpotomy/pulpectomy, topical application of fluoride, fissure sealant, stainless steel crowns, composite strip crowns, and extraction. Studies indicated that, irrespective of the treatment modality provided, substantial improvement has been established in the OHRQoL of the children with ECC. Along with the complexity of the dental treatment applied under general anesthesia, the timing of the post-test questionnaire, or, in other words, the follow-up period of the studies, may also affect the results. Theoretically, a post-test questionnaire on OHRQoL undertaken quickly after complex dental treatments, including many tooth extractions, may yield different results than a post-test questionnaire conducted after a relatively longer follow-up period. Post-operative discomfort and several adverse effects due to multiple tooth extractions, such as difficulty eating, impaired function, and so on, may persist for a short time after the procedure. In the study of Lee et al. [ 47 ], an increase in the scores for ‘child self-image’ and ‘social interaction’ subscales of the ECOHIS questionnaire was reported. The negative change was specific to these domains only and was attributed to the absence of teeth and its resulting adverse effects. The follow-up period of the studies included in this meta-analysis ranged from one week to 52.2 weeks. Long-term follow-up studies are needed to determine whether the impact on OHRQoL is sustained over time however, most of the studies included in this meta-analysis have a relatively short follow-up period, such as four weeks. Additionally, multiple measurements of OHRQoL at different time points during a relatively long follow-up period may also provide insights into the post-operative recovery process, such as how quickly quality of life recovers in cases of complex dental treatments involving multiple surgical procedures. Studies have assessed OHRQoL in children with a variety of medical conditions, and various reasons were reported for referring patients to receive dental treatment under general anesthesia. In several studies [ 22 – 24 , 28 , 32 , 34 , 37 – 44 , 46 , 50 , 51 , 54 – 56 ], dental treatment under general anesthesia was conducted only on healthy children with ECC, with no systemic diseases, mental problems, or disabilities, yet uncooperative due to very young age, high dental fear, and/or behavioral management problems and therefore were unable to accept treatment under local anesthesia. A study [ 26 ] reported that in addition to the pediatric patients’ dental fear and disability, the lack of time for multi-visit treatment was the cause for referring them to dental general anesthesia. Children in need of dental care under general anesthesia were either healthy or with mild to severe systemic diseases in several studies [ 27 , 29 , 35 ]. Some studies specifically focused on children with special health care needs [ 30 , 33 ]. Considering that the children receive indications for dental general anesthesia due to their young age, non-cooperative nature, and/or behavioral issues or disabilities, they cannot be expected to assess or express themselves regarding the change in their oral health and quality of life. Using child-reported measures in research presents several disadvantages. Children may struggle to accurately report their experiences, particularly regarding pain and quality of life, as their understanding and expression of these concepts can be uncertain and inconsistent, which is exacerbated in preschool-aged children due to the cognitive limitations at a young age [ 58 ]. Many quality-of-life questionnaires require a certain cognitive level, making them unsuitable for very young children, typically under six years old [ 45 ]. This inevitably makes it necessary for the questionnaire to be answered by parents or caregivers and makes proxy involvement crucial [ 59 ]. Proxy reports, provided by parents, caregivers, or family members, are widely used in evaluating the impact of a dental intervention on the OHRQoL of children. Nevertheless, potential discrepancies between proxy and child reports have raised concerns about whether the proxy perceptions and parental assessments could accurately reflect a child’s social and psychological well-being or real situation, due to their subjective nature and limited knowledge of the child’s experiences [ 59 – 61 ]. Considering these, several researchers highlighted the need for further high-quality studies combining both proxy and child-reported measures of OHRQoL to ensure a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of the child’s oral health experiences and to improve the validity and depth of the findings when analyzing the impact of various dental interventions on OHRQoL [ 60 , 62 ]. Nevertheless, research has shown that using age-specific questionnaires, such as the Early Childhood Oral Health Impact Scale (ECOHIS) for children under six and the Child Oral Health-Related Quality of Life (COHRQoL) for those aged 6 to 14, can yield more reliable data. Nevertheless, the age-specific questionnaires used in this meta-analysis, i.e., the ECOHIS for children under six and the COHRQoL for those aged 6 to 14, were demonstrated to yield more reliable data. The use of validated ECOHIS and COHRQoL tools proved to have good construct validity, internal consistency reliability, and test/retest reliability [ 11 , 14 , 63 ]. Additionally, the ECOHIS questionnaire has a “do not know” response to inhibit proxy overestimation of the treatment effects. Another notable concern is that for measuring the OHRQoL of children younger than six years old, several researchers [ 12 , 26 , 28 , 31 , 36 , 45 , 52 ] utilized the COHRQoL questionnaire, which was originally designed for children aged six to 14. However, for children younger than six years old, using the ECOHIS questionnaire would be more appropriate. This can be considered a limitation that prevents the comparability of relevant studies with other studies. In addition to the ECOHIS and COHRQoL tools, some additional tools, which are beyond the scope of this meta-analysis, were also presented in the studies, such as the DMFT (decayed, missing, and filled teeth) or DMFS (decayed, missing, and filled surface) indexes to present baseline caries experience [ 24 , 38 , 42 , 45 ], Plaque Index (PI) [ 30 ] for plaque presence assessment, anthropometric measurements included height, weight, and BMI calculations [ 23 ], Children’s Fear Survey Schedule-Dental Subscale (CFSS-DS) [ 25 , 29 , 45 , 46 ] for dental fear/dental anxiety measurement, Frankl behavior scale (FBS) [ 29 , 39 ] for assessing anxiety in children, Kessler-10 scale [ 37 ] for evaluating parents’ mental health status. Dental treatment under general anesthesia is clearly beneficial; however, it can lead to a variety of risks, complications and transient side effects, which are critical to understand for improving patient safety and outcomes. Complications associated with dental treatment of pediatric patients under general anesthesia can be influenced by factors such as patient age, underlying health conditions, and the nature of the dental procedure. Several researchers [ 64 ] reported that disabled pediatric patients experience more complications after dental treatment under general anesthesia, including oral bleeding, fever, diarrhea, and agitation, compared to healthy children. The most common complications identified in recent studies include respiratory issues such as laryngeal spasm and sore throat [ 65 , 66 ], emergence agitation [ 26 , 65 ], postoperative pain [ 65 ], and bleeding [ 65 ]. Some other complications are nausea and vomiting [ 26 , 28 , 52 ], fatigue and dizziness [ 28 , 52 ], headache [ 26 ], fever [ 26 ], and difficulty in mastication or speaking, especially after multiple extractions [ 65 ]. Less common but serious complications of general anesthesia include potential neurotoxicity, various medical morbidities, and mortality [ 48 , 67 ]. While general anesthesia is generally safe for pediatric dental procedures, the potential for complications necessitates careful preoperative assessment and postoperative monitoring to mitigate risks and to ensure patients’ safety and well-being. From the clinician’s perspective, dental treatments under general anesthesia should be considered the final therapeutic option rather than the treatment of first choice. The above-mentioned potential complications of dental general anesthesia, as well as medical, dental, legal, and financial consequences, should also be documented in clinical studies. Such studies can encourage parents and dentists to adopt preventive dental strategies to improve oral health-related quality of life and refrain from repeated dental treatments under general anesthesia by outlining potential complications and their medical, dental, legal, and financial consequences [ 4 ]. Limitations of the study As a limitation, this meta-analysis only focused on the studies using two validated and most commonly used tools, ECOHIS and COHRQoL. Additionally, the OHRQoL scores provided at the initial and last time points were addressed to assess the impact on OHRQoL. The lack of standardization regarding post-operative follow-up periods or post-test questionnaire timing and frequency in the included studies has directed the research to focus on the final outcome rather than the course of change in quality of life. As another limitation of this meta-analysis, the impacts of different dental treatment modalities on OHRQoL have not been addressed and should be considered when designing future research methods. Future research may aim to find an answer to the research question, “How do different treatment modalities performed under general anesthesia affect OHRQoL?” Post-operative complications and side effects associated with dental treatment of patients under general anesthesia can impact OHRQoL, yet this has not been evaluated within the scope of this study and constitutes another limitation. Additionally, the high diversity in the study designs due to a number of factors that cannot be standardized or controlled, such as age, ethnicity, patients’ initial oral health and medical status, type and complexity of dental treatments, operator impact on the quality of dental treatments or interventions, the facility of the health center, or duration of follow-up, etc., create a high level of heterogeneity and the limitation in this meta-analysis. Conclusions The findings of the studies included in this meta-analysis support that dental treatments under general anesthesia improved ECOHIS and COHRQoL scores in children with a significantly large effect size. In other words, dental treatments applied under general anesthesia and mentioned within the limitations of this meta-analysis improved children’s oral health-related quality of life in a period up to 52.2 weeks. Additionally, a positive effect on their families’ quality of life were detected. Future studies involving multiple scales with longer follow-up periods and providing quantitative and detailed data on the type of dental treatments and preventive dental strategies are needed. By accomplishing this, it may be possible to develop clearer clinical guidelines for dental general anesthesia, improve the informed consent process, and manage patients‘ and parents’ expectations. documents.title: Prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species and their multidrug resistance patterns among pediatric populations in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Salmonella and Shigella are major enteric pathogens that cause diarrhea in children worldwide. They are pathogenic microbes that cause significant diarrheal morbidity and mortality in under five children in resource limited countries. Thus, this systemic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species and their multidrug resistance patterns in pediatric populations in Ethiopia.
METHODS: The articles were searched extensively in the electronic databases and grey literature using entry terms or phrases. Studies meeting the eligibility criteria were extracted in MS Excel and exported for statistical analysis into STATA version 14 software. The overall pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species was computed using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and I2 statistics with corresponding p-values. Publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and Egger's test. In addition, sensitivity analysis was performed to determine the impact of individual studies on the pooled effect size.
RESULT: Of a total of 742 identified studies, 89 studies were eligible for full-text analysis. Of 89 studies, 21 were included for meta-analysis involving 5318 study participants. These eligible studies reported a total of 593 bacterial isolates. The overall pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella among pediatrics in Ethiopia was 10.70% (95% CI: 8.96-12.45), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 82.1%, p 2 of 95%, p < 0.0001 between the pooled prevalence of the two species.
CONCLUSION: The pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella and their multidrug resistance were alarmingly high in pediatric. The initial empirical treatment of pediatrics patients remains challenging and results high prevalence of antimicrobial resistance. Thus, appropriate infection prevention and control strategies should be implemented and treatment should be directed based on antimicrobial stewardship protocols.

They are pathogenic microbes that cause significant diarrheal morbidity and mortality in under five children in resource limited countries. Thus, this systemic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species and their multidrug resistance patterns in pediatric populations in Ethiopia. Methods The articles were searched extensively in the electronic databases and grey literature using entry terms or phrases. Studies meeting the eligibility criteria were extracted in MS Excel and exported for statistical analysis into STATA version 14 software. The overall pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species was computed using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and I 2 statistics with corresponding p -values. Publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and Egger’s test. In addition, sensitivity analysis was performed to determine the impact of individual studies on the pooled effect size. Result Of a total of 742 identified studies, 89 studies were eligible for full-text analysis. Of 89 studies, 21 were included for meta-analysis involving 5318 study participants. These eligible studies reported a total of 593 bacterial isolates. The overall pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella among pediatrics in Ethiopia was 10.70% (95% CI: 8.96–12.45), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 82.1%, p < 0.001) across the studies. The pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella individually among pediatrics in Ethiopia was 15.43% (95% CI: 10.42–20.72) and 15.83% (95% CI: 11.40–20.40), respectively. Moreover, the overall prevalence of multidrug resistance in Salmonella and Shigella isolates was 81.03% (95% CI: 77.39–84.67) with substantial heterogeneity of I 2 of 95%, p < 0.0001 between the pooled prevalence of the two species. Conclusion The pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella and their multidrug resistance were alarmingly high in pediatric. The initial empirical treatment of pediatrics patients remains challenging and results high prevalence of antimicrobial resistance. Thus, appropriate infection prevention and control strategies should be implemented and treatment should be directed based on antimicrobial stewardship protocols. Salmonella is a type of bacteria that can cause salmonellosis, a condition marked by diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and cramping. Salmonella infections in children typically cause diarrhea (sometimes with blood), fever, and stomach pain [ 1 ]. Infections can be more severe in young children and people with weakened immune systems, causing infections in the blood (called bacteremia), bones, joints, or brain. Salmonella infections are usually caused by eating or drinking contaminated food with the faeces of an infected animal. Shigella bacteria can also cause shigellosis, which is characterized by diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramps [ 1 ]. Salmonella and Shigella are major enteric pathogens that cause diarrhea in children worldwide. Diarrheal diseases caused by Salmonella and Shigella result in high levels of morbidity and mortality, particularly in under-five children. Salmonella and Shigella are pathogenic microbes that cause the majority of diarrheal deaths. Children aged one to three years were significantly more likely to be infected with these bacteria [ 2 ]. Children whose parents did not have waste disposal facilities and raised domestic animals were more likely to have Salmonella and Shigella isolates. Resistance patterns for commonly prescribed antimicrobials have varied in Salmonella and Shigella strains isolated from African children, making treatment more difficult [ 3 ]. Salmonella and Shigella strains isolated from children have developed multidrug resistance to a variety of antibiotics, including ampicillin, amoxicillin, tetracycline, cotrimoxazole, and chloramphenicol. Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, azithromycin, and ceftriaxone are some other antibiotics that are effective in treating Shigella infections. Ciprofloxacin is the first-line treatment for Shigella dysentery , according to the World Health Organization. Because antibiotic resistance patterns vary by region and over time, local susceptibility testing is recommended to guide treatment decisions [ 4 – 6 ]. In Southern Ethiopia, the overall prevalence of Salmonella infection among under-five children was 12.6%. Shigella bacteria, which can cause an intestinal infection called shigellosis, were resistant to commonly prescribed antibiotics such as amoxicillin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, clindamycin, norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, and, gentamycin [ 7 ]. Shigella infection is highly contagious and can be spread through contact with an infected person’s stool or contaminated items. Shigellosis is most common in under-five children, but it can affect all age groups. Shigellosis symptoms include diarrhea, stomach pain and cramps, vomiting, and fever. Shigella infection has been linked to death in children who have diarrhea [ 8 ]. In Ethiopia, a systematic review found a pooled prevalence of 6.6%, with the highest rates in health facilities and lower rates in community. Resistance was high to ampicillin, amoxicillin, and erythromycin, while lower resistance was noted for ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone [ 9 ]. Salmonella and Shigella are pathogenic microbes that cause significant diarrheal mortality in under-five children. Shigella and Salmonella were causing diarrhea in 7.6% of children in Southern Ethiopia [ 10 ]. The prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species was 6.9% and 4.3%, respectively, among diarrheic under-five children in Ethiopia [ 6 ]. In Ethiopia the overall prevalence of culture-confirmed Salmonella and Shigella infection among under-five children was 11.7% [ 11 ]. In addition, the overall prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella infection was 3.8% in Ethiopia [ 5 ]. A study in Ethiopia documented that 9.3% of under-five children with diarrheal diseases were positive for bacterial growth, with Shigella and Salmonella species accounting for 8.3% and 1%, respectively [ 12 ]. In another study conducted in Adama, Ethiopia, Salmonella (4.5%) and Shigella (3.5%) species were identified among diarrhea patients, and high proportion of antibiotic resistance was reported [ 13 ]. Methods Design and protocol registration This systematic review and meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 14 ]. The protocol for this review was initially registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) database with the registration identification number CRD42023444166. Search strategies and selection of studies A comprehensive systematic literature review was conducted in Ethiopia between May 1 and June 30, 2023, to gather data on Salmonella and Shigella prevalence and multidrug resistance (MDR). The search included electronic databases (PubMed/Medline, Science Direct, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science), grey literature sources (Google Scholar, African Journal Online, ResearchGate, university repositories), and a Google search of reference lists from included studies. Eligible studies published between January 2000 and April 30, 2023, were considered for inclusion. The searching strategy utilized Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and combinations of keywords such as “prevalence”, “epidemiology”, “burden”, “incidence”, “ Shigella ”, “ Salmonella ”, “antibiotic resistance”, “antibiotic susceptibility”, “multidrug resistance”, “children”, “pediatrics”, and “Ethiopia”, employing Boolean operators (“OR” and “AND”) as necessary in advanced database searches. Eligibility criteria We created a study eligibility checklist before identifying peer-reviewed and published full-text articles in local or international journals about the prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species and their antimicrobial resistance profile in pediatric populations in Ethiopia. The inclusion criteria include laboratory-based observational (e.g., cross-sectional) studies, drug sensitivity testing performed in a laboratory setting with defined cut-offs for antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), studies written in English, studies conducted in Ethiopia from human/clinical specimens, and online availability between January 2010 and May 2024. Qualitative studies, reviews, letters to the editor, author responses, commentaries, studies using environmental or animal samples, and studies that did not specify the number of isolates studied were all excluded furthermore, studies with missing interest-related outcomes. Data extraction Five reviewers (MT, AGB, MAB, ZM, and HD) independently extracted data from eligible studies in Microsoft Excel sheets. The information extracted from each study includes the first author’s name, publication year, setting, region, type of sample, sample size, type of bacterial isolate, number of isolates, and MDR status. Search results were consolidated into Endnote 20 software (Clarivate Analytics USA) and duplicates were removed. Five independent reviewers (MT, MAB, AS, BE, and HE) identified the articles from databases and other sources. Duplicates were removed and five independent reviewers (MAB, HD, SGS, OM, HE) screened the titles and abstracts of all retrieved studies which were double-checked by a third reviewer (AGB and AS). The full texts of potentially eligible studies were evaluated in detail against the inclusion criteria by five reviewers (MT, BE, MAB, DGW, and EA), double-checked by two reviewers (MAB and AS), and added to the extraction collection. Any disagreements among reviewers throughout each stage of screening were unraveled through discussion or with the intruding of three reviewers (SGS, EA, and HE). Quality assessment The quality of the articles was carefully evaluated by four authors. The full texts of the articles were used to determine whether the study met the selection criteria or if the article’s eligibility was questioned. Each study design was evaluated for methodological validity using the Joanna Brigg Institute (JBI) quality assessment manual [ 15 , 16 ]. Using the critical appraisal checklists, studies were reviewed, and articles with an average score of 50–75% were considered to be of good quality, while scores greater than 75% were defined as high quality. This systematic review and meta-analysis included articles of both good and high quality. Furthermore, studies with missing or vague outcomes of interest, as well as those lacking explicit method descriptions, were excluded. Outcome variables The main focus of this study was to determine the combined prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species in cases of diarrheal diseases. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the overall prevalence of multidrug resistance among these species in pediatric populations across Ethiopia. Data processing and analysis The data were analyzed with STATA version 14.0 statistical software. A random effect model was used to calculate the pooled estimate and MDR of the isolates. A potential source of heterogeneity was investigated using subgroup and meta-regression analyses. The Cochran’s Q test and I 2 statistics were used to quantify and assess the degree of heterogeneity among studies. The presence of heterogeneity was determined using I 2 statistics with a p -value < 0.001 [ 17 ] and the Der Simonian-Laired random effects model was employed [ 16 , 18 ]. The results were presented as a table and a forest plot. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plot symmetry and Egger’s test statistics. Trim-and-fill was used in asymmetrical funnel plots to combine missing studies and estimate adjusted effect size. Meta-regression was used to further assess the cause of heterogeneity. Result Selection and identification of studies A total of 742 articles were retrieved from databases. About 350 articles remained after removing 392 duplicate articles. The remaining, 261 articles were excluded after reviewing the title, abstract, and objective of the study. Finally, 89 full-length articles were thoroughly reviewed by predetermined eligibility criteria, and 21 studies were included in the meta-analysis (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram illustrating the process of selecting eligible studies for the systematic review and meta-analysis Study characteristics Table 1 Summarizes the characteristics of 21 studies included in our final meta-analysis. These studies were conducted between 2010 and 2024 in different regions of Ethiopia and were used to estimate the pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species in Ethiopia [ 6 , 7 , 11 , 12 , 19 – 26 ]. The studies involved 5318 study participants. The sample size of the studies ranged from 22 to 422. The studies were conducted in one city administration and three national regional states of Ethiopia. All the included studies employed a cross-sectional study design. Among 593 reported bacterial isolates, 309 and 284 isolates were Salmonella and Shigella species, respectively (Table 1 ). Multi-drug-resistant Salmonella and Shigella species are well noted for their ability to spread rapidly and become a global public health threat [ 33 – 35 ]. This can be associated with the emergence of multidrug-resistant strains that have seriously harmed public health, especially in resource-limited countries. In this study, the overall pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species identified from stool samples of pediatric populations in Ethiopia was 10.70% (95% CI: 8.96–12.45). The findings of the present studies imply that infection due to Salmonella and Shigella in pediatric populations have been continued as major public health significance. Based on the available studies, this revealed that 1 in 10 pediatrics are infected at any given time in Ethiopia. Thus, the findings of the meta-analysis summarize that the infections are in agreement with global evidence reported that 190 million pediatrics were infected with these bacterial pathogens. These statistics figures elicit the multisectoral coordination efforts of health workers, policymakers, and communities to reduce the transmissions of these pathogens from contaminated foods. Because of children at this age are naturally taking contaminated soils, food and water into their mouth and may acquire disease causing microbes and rural areas were more susceptible to diarrhea due to Salmonella and Shigella infection than the counterparts [ 36 – 38 ]. So, policy makers and public health workers create awareness creation on daily personal hygiene and environmental sanitation practices and reduce the provision of health facilities in rural areas compared to urban areas. Furthermore, the pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species among pediatrics populations in Ethiopia was 15.43% (95% CI: 10.42–20.72) and 15.83% (95% CI: 11.40–20.40), respectively. The finding of this evidence was higher than previous evidence of shigellosis in children (7%), while in adult populations (2.2%) [ 9 ] and in Ethiopia, a systematic review found a pooled prevalence of 6.6% [ 9 ]. The higher prevalence of Shigella in children in comparison with adults suggests an increased susceptibility of children to Shigella infection, which may be due to unsanitary food handling practices, compromised sanitation, malnutrition, and the ability to cause disease with a small inoculum and facilitate person to person transmission. Individual studies included in this systematic review and meta-analysis revealed significant variation in the prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species infections in Ethiopia, depending on the bacterial species, geographical region, patient type, and sample size. Furthermore, this review revealed that Salmonella and Shigella species were more distributed in Ethiopia’s central region (Addis Abeba), followed by Ethiopia’s Amhara and Oromia regions. According to the findings of this meta-analysis, a high pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species was detected in Ethiopia. This showed that salmonellosis and shigellosis infections among pediatrics groups are increasing, which might be linked to drinking an unimproved water sources, absence of latrine, absence of hand washing habits before meals and after toilet by parents, and unimmunized children [ 6 ]. The emergence of MDR strains represents a significant threat, not only to the pediatrics population but also to the hospital settings and the general populations in Ethiopia as well as in Africa and the globe due to the dissemination of resistance genes via immigration and tourism. Thus, the emergence of this resistance has been a global health concern [ 39 ]. This is consistent with an increasing trend of Salmonella and Shigella species isolates globally [ 40 ]. In this review, a total of 309 Salmonella species were identified, including 12 S. typhi , 10 S. paratyphi , and 287 unidentified strains, reflecting the complexity of these infections. In Ethiopia, 284 Shigella species were reported among pediatric patients, with S. flexneri (56 cases) and S. dysenteriae (54 cases) being most prevalent, and 160 strains remaining unidentified. These findings underscore the urgent need for improved diagnostic techniques and surveillance to better understand these pathogens’ epidemiology. Additionally, the common occurrence of Non-Typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) in gastroenteritis, often without symptoms, complicates identification and management, further emphasizing the necessity for ongoing research and monitoring efforts [ 41 ]. The magnitude of Salmonella and Shigella species infections and their MDR patterns in this meta-analysis study indicated the need for timely response to antimicrobial resistance through different modalities, such as appropriate antibiotic use and regulation strategies and antimicrobial stewardship programs, to combat the antibiotic resistance burden in Ethiopia. Furthermore, the overall pooled prevalence of MDR was 81.03% (95% CI: 77.39–84.67) with substantial heterogeneity of I 2 of 95%, p < 0.0001. This systematic review was comparable with studies reported in Ethiopia like in Bahir Dar (82%) [ 19 ], Debremarkos (82%) [ 11 ], and Ambo (84%) [ 5 ], but higher than other studies documented in Mekelle (94.6%) [ 23 ], Hawassa (93.3%) [ 25 ], Addis Ababa (92%) [ 26 ]. The possible causes of higher MDR may be incomplete treatment or routine practice of empirical treatment of children, poor adherence to medication regimens, overuse, poor sanitation, and inadequate infection prevention. Variations may also be due to differences in factors such as access to healthcare, sanitation, and agricultural practices may play a role in determining geographical hotspots and resource allocations. This finding also highlights the importance of integrated antimicrobial surveillance efforts, as well as the potential for national policy and guideline changes, emphasizing the importance of appropriate diagnosis and treatment protocols. MDR is a significant problem in pediatric populations worldwide. Studies reported that the rate of MDR for Salmonella ranges from 20 to 80%, and Shigella from 30 to 90% [ 42 ]. In this systematic and meta-analysis study, the pooled MDR rate for Salmonella and S higella species was 78.35% (95% CI: 76.84–79.58) and 79.67% (95% CI: 74.75–83.25), respectively. The MDR rate of Salmonella isolates in this review was consistent. The treatment of diarrheal diseases caused by Salmonella and Shigella species should consider the age restrictions associated with usage of certain antimicrobials in children. Substantial heterogeneity with an I 2 of 95.7% for Salmonella species and 95.7% for Shigella species was detected in this study. This high heterogeneity observed in this study is more likely not only due to publication bias but also differences in IPC practices of health facilities, and methodological issues such as sample size, method of identification, methods of antimicrobial sensitivity testing, variation in study settings, periodic variation of studies, immunity status and underlining conditions of patients. Sensitivity analysis, and meta-regression have been carried out to rule out the most possible causes of heterogeneity. The results of sensitivity analysis proved that there is no single study that impacted the pooled effect size. The pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species infections in Ethiopia was determined by omitting each study sequentially and the computed pooled prevalence was within 95% CI of the overall pooled prevalence. Meta-regression has been confirmed that the number of bacterial isolates had a significant cause of heterogeneity in Salmonella and Shigella species while publication year, geographic region, sample size, and total isolates were not a cause. In addition, publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot confirming the presence of publication bias and Egger’s test statistics, indicating the absence of publication bias. This review has certain limitations such as heterogeneity of studies included to estimate of pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species. Therefore, to limit the influence of the study heterogeneity, the random-effects model of Sidik-Jonkmann was implemented in the meta-analyses, and subgroup analyses, sensitivity analysis and meta-regression were also performed. Conclusion According to this systematic review and meta-analysis, the pooled prevalence of Salmonella and Shigella species infections has alarmingly increased and become a public health threat. This indicates the burden of Salmonella and Shigella species infections urges the need for routine screening and appropriate treatment for better management and effective control of drug resistant strains transmission. Furthermore, it serves as a wake-up call to international, continental, and national health bureaus, and other stakeholders to develop targeted IPC strategies. This finding is also an alert call for stakeholders to develop strong antibiotic stewardship programs in the healthcare systems. documents.title: Clinical Patterns of Osteoarticular, Bone Marrow and Urogenital Paracoccidioidomycosis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Paracoccidioidomycosis (PCM) is an endemic systemic mycosis in Latin America, classically characterized by pulmonary, mucosal and lymphatic involvement. Extrapulmonary manifestations affecting uncommon organs remain poorly characterized and may contribute to diagnostic delay and adverse outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective case series of proven or probable atypical extrapulmonary PCM diagnosed at a Brazilian tertiary referral center between 2006 and 2025. A systematic review registered in PROSPERO and conducted according to PRISMA recommendations identified osteoarticular, bone marrow and urogenital PCM cases between 1970 to November 2025 in PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase without language restrictions.
RESULTS: Among 205 PCM patients evaluated at our institution, 14 (6.8%) presented atypical extrapulmonary involvement. Combined with 153 cases identified in 75 studies, 167 cases were analysed. Osteoarticular involvement was the most frequent manifestation (53.9%), predominantly affecting young patients with acute/subacute disease and presenting mainly as osteomyelitis with lytic lesions. Bone marrow involvement occurred exclusively in acute/subacute PCM and was associated with post-mortem diagnosis (9.7%) and markedly elevated mortality (77.8%). Urogenital PCM mainly affected middle-aged men with chronic disease, frequently involving the testicles and prostate, and was associated with delayed diagnosis, surgical intervention (32.7%), and mortality (32.0%). Distinct epidemiological profiles, clinical forms and outcomes were consistently observed across atypical sites.
CONCLUSION: Atypical extrapulmonary PCM manifestations follow recognizable clinical patterns associated with diagnostic delay and poor outcomes, supporting earlier investigation and timely antifungal therapy in endemic settings.
documents.conclusions: Atypical extrapulmonary PCM manifestations follow recognizable clinical patterns associated with diagnostic delay and poor outcomes, supporting earlier investigation and timely antifungal therapy in endemic settings.

Introduction Paracoccidioidomycosis (PCM) is a systemic infection caused by species of the Paracoccidioides brasiliensis complex and Paracoccidioides lutzii . PCM is a prevalent and endemic infection throughout Central and South America, with around 80% of cases documented in Brazil [ 1 ]. Between 1930 and 2012, more than 15,000 cases were registered in Latin America [ 2 ]. However, this number only partially illustrates the actual burden of this mycosis. The absence of compulsory notification and underdiagnosis contribute to the hardship in accurately tracking its epidemiology. Primary infection usually is asymptomatic and normally occurs in the first two decades of life [ 1 ]. When it causes disease, PCM can present in two distinct clinical forms. The most common is the chronic form, which typically affects adults between 30 and 60 years of age and is characterized by pulmonary involvement and lesions of the upper aerodigestive tract mucosa [ 1 , 3 ]. The acute/subacute form is more frequently observed in individuals under 30 years of age and primarily involves the reticuloendothelial system, being characterized by fever, localized or generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly [ 1 , 3 ]. PCM infection can be easily mistaken for other diseases due to its capacity to disseminate and involve virtually any organ or system. While typical cases are well documented in the literature, the presentation and characterization of atypical PCM sites remain highly variable, even in endemic regions such as Brazil [ 3 ]. This variability can lead to diagnostic delays and contribute to the increased morbidity and mortality associated with the disease [ 1 ]. Most descriptions of atypical cases come from case reports with unusual pulmonary and cutaneous presentations [ 4 , 5 ]. Nonetheless, little is known about the involvement of rare sites by the disease, such as the osteoarticular, bone marrow and urogenital systems. At the same time, there are no studies defining what constitutes atypical or rare site involvement in PCM. Therefore, this study reports a case series of rare PCM sites from a Brazilian reference center and systematically reviews published cases of atypical sites in PCM, emphasizing their main epidemiological and clinical characteristics. 2. Methods This was a retrospective study with secondary data analysis. We included cases of proven or probable PCM at atypical sites, diagnosed at the Hospital das Clínicas, Faculty of Medicine, University of São Paulo (HCFMUSP), between 2006 and 2025. Proven cases are characterized by patients with clinical manifestations compatible with PCM, in whom typical yeast forms of Paracoccidioides species have been identified in any clinical sample through direct mycological examination, culture or histopathology. Probable cases are marked by suggestive clinical manifestations and the detection of specific antibodies in serum, but without identification of Paracoccidioides species in clinical samples [ 1 ]. Atypical forms comprised organ involvements not classically recognized as typical PCM manifestations in current consensus guidelines and major reviews of the disease, where pulmonary, mucosal, lymphatic and cutaneous involvements predominate [ 1 , 3 ]. Therefore, we defined atypical sites as clinical involvement occurring in fewer than 5% of cases. Then, a literature review was performed, following the PRISMA guidelines [ 6 ], using the databases PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase, which were last consulted in November 2025. Studies were retrieved using the terms described in the Appendix A . We did not use any restrictions regarding languages. Aiming to expand the search, references of the selected articles were reviewed to find additional articles. We registered the protocol on PROSPERO (CRD420261302185). Two qualified investigators (WLLK and MCS) independently assessed the eligibility of the identified publications and discrepancies were resolved by discussion. We first performed an initial screen of titles or abstracts to assess potential relevance. Afterward, we obtained relevant full‐text articles, reevaluated their eligibility and determined their final inclusion or exclusion. Criteria for inclusion were articles: (i) reporting proven or probable PCM; (ii) describing atypical PCM manifestations (osteoarticular, bone marrow and urogenital); (iii) published between 1970 and November 2025. If there was more than one study published using the same case, the most recent study was selected for analysis. We excluded reviews, studies with animals, and in vitro studies. We employed a standardized pilot‐tested data collection form that comprised the publication year, country, age, sex, occupation, smoking, alcoholism, comorbidities, clinical form (acute/subacute or chronic), clinical manifestations, duration of symptoms, tissue/organ involvement, diagnosis method (direct microscopy, culture, histology and serology), autopsy, hospitalization, antifungal therapy, surgical treatment and outcomes (improvement and death). We evaluated specific findings regarding the individual patient data collected on atypical forms. In osteoarticular PCM, cases were categorized as arthritis, osteomyelitis, tenosynovitis/bursitis and/or myositis. Arthritis was classified as monoarticular (one joint involved), oligoarticular (two to four joints involved) and polyarticular (more than four joints involved). The other conditions (osteomyelitis, tenosynovitis/bursitis and myositis) were classified as unifocal (a single affected site) and multifocal (more than one affected site). Additional signs and symptoms assessed included local pain, edema, hyperemia and fistula formation. For a more comprehensive assessment, we included magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), ultrasound (USG) and X‐ray. Radiological abnormalities comprised joint effusion, synovitis, abscess, soft tissue edema, lytic lesions and periosteal reaction. Cases were categorized as genital, renal, or urinary tract involvement in urogenital PCM, with documentation of unilateral or bilateral disease. Signs and symptoms assessed included genital lesions, urgency, nocturia, hematuria, pollakiuria, dysuria, urinary retention, local pain and edema. In cases with bone marrow involvement, the presence of anaemia, pancytopenia and eosinophilia was evaluated. Simple descriptive statistics, such as the mean and Standard Deviation (SD), frequency and median, were used to characterize the data. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the local ethics committee (Approval date: 09/11/2024; approval file: 7000069187). Informed consent was waived because this study was retrospective, with the review of medical records. 3. Results 3.1. Case Series A total of 205 patients with proven or probable PCM at HCFMUSP between 2006 and 2025 were analysed, of whom 14 (6.8%) presented with atypical involvement, including osteoarticular, bone marrow and urogenital sites. Of these, 10 (71.4%) had osteoarticular involvement, 3 (21.4%) had bone marrow involvement, and 4 (28.6%) had urogenital involvement, with some patients presenting overlapping involvement across sites. The median age was 40 years (range: 4–66), with 11 males (78.6%) and 3 females (21.4%). Only one patient was immunocompromised, receiving azathioprine and hydroxychloroquine for systemic lupus erythematosus. Other reported comorbidities included diabetes mellitus (2 [14.3%]), heart disease (2 [14.3%]), tuberculosis (1 [7.1%]) and cirrhosis (1 [7.1%]) (Table 1 ). Most cases presented with the acute/subacute clinical form (8 [57.1%]), after a median delay of 13 weeks (range: 1–52 weeks) from symptom onset. All patients had multifocal organ involvement, with weight loss (11 [78.6%]) and fever (10 [71.4%]) being the most common presenting symptoms. In cases with osteoarticular involvement, local pain (4 [40.0%]), local edema (2 [20.0%]) and fistula formation (1 [10.0%]) were observed; no patient presented with local hyperemia. Unifocal osteomyelitis (5 [50.0%]) and multifocal osteomyelitis (5 [50.0%]) were the most common clinical presentations, followed by monoarthritis (2 [20.0%]). The most frequently affected sites were the rib (3 [30.0%]) and clavicle (3 [30.0%]); other sites included the knee (2 [20.0%]), vertebrae (2 [20.0%]), sternum, manubriosternal joint, ilium, tibia and scapula (1 [10.0%] each). CT and X‐ray were performed in all cases, and MRI in two cases (2 [20.0%]). Radiological findings included lytic lesions (10 [100%]), soft tissue edema (3 [30.0%]), abscess formation (1 [10.0%]), synovitis (1 [10.0%]) and joint effusion (1 [10.0%]). No periosteal reaction was observed. In urogenital PCM, no patient presented with urinary urgency, nocturia, hematuria, pollakiuria, dysuria, or urinary retention. Cutaneous lesions were observed in two cases (2 [50.0%]), both presenting as ulcers. Local pain and local edema were reported in three (3 [75.0%]) and one (1 [25.0%]) patient, respectively. The testicle was the most commonly affected site (3 [75.0%]), all with unilateral involvement. The epididymis and penis were each involved in one case (1 [25.0%]). Laboratory abnormalities for all atypical forms were summarized in Table 1 . Diagnostic methods included mycological direct exam, culture, histopathology and serology. No patient received a post‐mortem diagnosis; however, in one case, testicular involvement was identified only at autopsy. A specific microbiological diagnosis at the atypical site was achieved in only half of the cases. In the remaining patients, diagnosis was established based on microbiological confirmation at another site combined with clinical and/or radiological findings. Serology was positive in all patients. Table 1 summarizes the diagnostic methods used. The majority of patients required hospitalization (12 [85.7%]), whereas surgical intervention was required in a minority of cases, all of which were orchiectomies (2 [14.3%]). Antifungal therapy was administered to 13 patients (13 [92.9%]), with intravenous amphotericin B used in five cases (5 [35.7%]). Additional antifungal agents included itraconazole (7 [50.0%]), sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim (SMX–TMP) (4 [28.6%]) and ketoconazole (1 [7.1%]). Outcome data were available for 11 patients; among them, three (27.3%) died and eight (72.7%) showed clinical improvement. 3.2. Systematic Review The final review included 75 articles published between 1970 and 2025, describing a total of 153 cases. Overlapping involvement of atypical sites was observed in five cases: one involving bone marrow, osteoarticular and urogenital systems; two involving bone marrow and osteoarticular sites; one involving bone marrow and urogenital sites; and one involving urogenital and osteoarticular sites. A flowchart illustrating the search strategy is shown in Figure 1 . When combining our case series with the literature review ( n = 167 total cases), the majority of cases were from Brazil (151 [90.4%]), followed by the United States (4 [2.4%]) and Colombia (3 [1.8%]). FIGURE 1 Flowchart describing the total of scientific articles obtained by the database searches for atypical paracoccidioidomycosis cases. 3.3. Osteoarticular We identified 10 cases of PCM with osteoarticular involvement over a 19‐year period (Table 1 ). The PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase searches identified 80 additional cases up to November 2025. The median age of cases with osteoarticular involvement was 29 years (range: 3–82), with a predominance of males (71/87 [81.6%]) and the acute/subacute clinical form (51/85 [60.0%]) (Table 2 ). Among patients with available data, most were previously healthy (49 [70.0%]). Among those with comorbidities (21 [30.0%]), the most frequent conditions were heart disease (6 [28.6%]), HIV infection (4 [19.0%]; median CD4 count: 94 cells/mm 3 ; range: 9–291), tuberculosis (3 [14.3%]), diabetes mellitus (2 [9.5%]), autoimmune diseases (2 [9.5%]), prior solid organ transplantation (2 [9.5%]), haematological malignancies (2 [9.5%]), chronic kidney disease (1 [4.8%]) and cirrhosis (1 [4.8%]).
